answer: Use the sc-rx command, which shows Receiving Secure Channel attributes. Syntax: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The state attribute is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack and takes two values: in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, and not-in-use, meaning no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use. name is the entity name, a string of length 0..64; index is the Receiving Secure Channel Index, a uint8; sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier as a hex-string of length 16. sc-rx is show-only: there is no add, set or delete form. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is read-only: the only form is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. There is no add, set or delete for sc-tx, so it cannot be configured; the values are reported by the MKA stack. name is the entity name, a string of length 0..64; index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index, a uint8; sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16; state is either in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, or not-in-use, meaning none are in use. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign the certificate with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>, where id is a string of length 0..20 and active-certificate-id is a string of length 0..128 that may list several certificates, for example set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. The in-use attribute is a leafref to ../active-certificate-id and shows the certificate actually active. To require a client certificate, set verify-client-cert, which enables or disables TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled means no client certificate is requested, required means the client certificate is required and validated. Default is disabled; for TLS Mutual Authentication it must be required. Changes only affect new TLS connections, not existing ones. show secure-application-<id> reports type (server or client), status (enabled or disabled), active-certificate-id, in-use and verify-client-cert; show secure-applications lists them all.

Only if you tell it to. The secure-entity attribute re-key-fail-policy indicates the NE policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful. Its values are kill-traffic and continue-traffic, and the default is continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to this IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0, that is, immediately. Related, re-key-frequency is 3600..86400 seconds with a default of 28800. All three can be given on add secure-entity-<name> or changed later with set secure-entity-<name>, for example add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity 1-4-L1-1 re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. There is no add or set form, and every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521, the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer. The proposal number is likewise the single value 1, defaulting to 1, and name is the proposal name for the secure entity SA. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the IKE peer itself. Commands: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>], plus matching set, show and delete forms. ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance; ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object, that is the IKE SA; associated-secure-entity is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). All three are strings with no stated default. Example: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with a manually configured CRL Distribution Point (CDP); each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Use add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], with set, show, delete cdp, delete cdp-<name> and show cdps. url is an HTTP URL in the form http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>, host being an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the file conventionally having a .crl extension, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true, false, default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh and immediately triggers a CRL auto-download; when disabled no refresh occurs but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval is either the enum use-next-update, taking the time from the current CRL next-update field, or a duration written as [xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs], for example 2w or 5d 12h or 1h 7m 30s. show also returns next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Privilege level is System Administrator.

Use cert-gen, which generates a self-signed certificate in Operational mode: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. Validity is set by days, the number of days a certificate is valid for, and the default is 365. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128, org-name a string of length 1..64, common-name the IP or host name identifying the server, string 1..64, and subject the full certificate subject name, string 1..1024. You must specify either subject or common-name when generating the self-signed certificate. auto-install (true, false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application without an active certificate. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, a prioritized set of rules that map an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Use add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>], with set, show and delete forms. map-type is either extract, to take the identity from a designated certificate field, or map, to use an explicit username. field applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and gives the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked; priority ranges 1 to 255; issuer adds a restriction filtering certificates from a specific issuer, value any; enabled is True or False, default True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Delete with clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>, run from Operational mode; -f forces without confirmation, otherwise the CLI prompts Are you sure? [y/n]. type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID, a string of length 0..128, which must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to list the certificate-ids that can be cleared. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY. type also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, use show certificates, which displays all managed local, trusted and peer X509v3 certificates imported by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations.

Use clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value> and pick the right clear-target. The choices are single-crl, the default, which removes only the CRL named in <crl-name> (for single-crl the crl-name is mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL); purge-invalid-crls, which purges all invalid CRLs; purge-cached-crls, which purges all CRLs automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension; and purge-all-crls, which purges every CRL. So to drop stale ones only, use clear crl purge-invalid-crls; purge-all-crls would take the good ones too. Press <tab> for the list of clearable CRL names; otherwise crl-name should be omitted. Check status first with show crls or show crl-<name>, whose status attribute is valid, expired or future, and whose type attribute is cached or manually. Access Mode is Operational mode, with Candidate Configuration mode allowed for the show command only.

csr-gen generates a Certificate Signing Request from user-provided information. The consequence of the command is the creation of a local-certificate in the pending-import state, plus the output of a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then given to an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that import happens, show local-certificate-<id> reports status pending-import, defined as a certificate generated by CSR whose import is not yet complete. Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=] [SAN=] [key-usage=] [extended-key-usage=]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256, metadata-template to generic, key-usage to digitalSignature,keyAgreement and extended-key-usage to serverAuth,clientAuth. Run from Operational mode. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type defines the requested type of display operation and takes all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details or certificate-hierarchy, with all-certificate-hierarchy as the default. So certificate-hierarchy gives the chain for the named certificate, all-certificate-hierarchy the full hierarchy, and certificate-details only the certificate own contents. certificate is the certificate to display, a string; tab completion lists the installed names such as local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert, trusted-certificate-ca_root and trusted-certificate-pace_root, for example display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root. The command shows details of a certificate or CSR and runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related local-certificate and peer-certificate objects also expose a trust-chain attribute listing the trusted certificates that constitute the trust chain.

Use the est command, the Enrollment over Secure Transport client, which automates certificate requests, renewals and management over HTTPS and replaces the manual CSR process. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=] [SAN=] [key-usage=] [extended-key-usage=] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is the key choice: cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca is the CA set for EST, default 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072 or rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic and also accepts from-existing-certificate, from-openssl-cnf, generic-tls-server, generic-tls-client and generic-ikev2-identity. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>], with a matching show. auto-re-enrollment specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by this EST CA. Accepted values are a number of days before expiration, from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the elapsed certificate lifetime, that is of the not-after minus not-before interval rounded up, from 10% to 90% in 10% increments, or disabled. The default is disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example by expiring. The CA is pinned by root-fingerprint, which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection, alongside explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port defaults to 443. Configure with add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], plus set, delete and show forms. server-address is the IP address of the EST server and server-port its port number, default 443. Yes, you can define more than one: each server is keyed by <name>/<server-name> and priority defines the server precedence, range 1 to 10. If priority is omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence, that is the highest existing number, plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. enabled is True or False, default True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base URL, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE directly, from Operational mode. Syntax: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]; import-certificate -h displays help. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by in the system. The PEM string carries the certificate(s) and, where applicable, private keys; passphrase decodes encrypted input certificates and applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle in addition to the leaf, and for single-certificate files imports intermediates referenced through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix. Example: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>.

Check the ISK attributes before clearing. show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], and show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates whether the key is in use in this FRU, true or false, default false. is-key-verified indicates whether the key is verified in this FRU, true or false, default false. being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, meaning the system is in the process of deletion and will soon delete this ISK; otherwise it is false. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. Remove one with clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, where key-name is a string of length 0..64 and must be supplied; -f forces the command without confirmation. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1, then clear isk key-name=name.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys (KRKs) and KRK information. Two forms: show KRKs for the whole list, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] for one key, for example show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1. name is the unique representation of the object; CPU is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0, a uint8; key-name is the name of the key, a string of length 0..64; key-serial-number is the Key Serial Number; issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20; key-length is the key length in bits, a uint16; key-payload is the key payload in hex format, a string of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. It shows the key replacement package (KRP) attributes and is show-only. KRP-version is the package version; key-name is the name of the resource; issuer-name is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), string length 0..20; KRK-name is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK; signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string 0..1024; signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. install-status indicates whether the KRP has been installed in the system and takes not-installed, installing, installed or failed. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute on the local-certificate object: set local-certificate-<id> revocation-mode <value>. It controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, with auto as the default. force-revoked makes the node treat the certificate as revoked; force-unrevoked forces the opposite. The same set command also accepts alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (string 0..256). id is a unique object identifier for the certificate, a string of length 1..128. Verify with show local-certificate-<id>, which returns revocation-mode along with status, whose values include revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future and valid, plus used-by, the list of secure-applications, ikev2-peers and similar presently using the certificate, and trust-chain and self-signed. The identical revocation-mode attribute, same values and same auto default, exists on peer-certificate. Certificates are deleted with the clear certificate command.

Add the responder with add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], and adjust later with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>]; delete ocsp-server-<name> removes it. priority sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones. Its range is uint8 1..10. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form http://<host>[:<port>], where host is an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the port is optional, defaulting to HTTP port 80, for example http://ocsp.example.org; it is a string of length 0..1024. enabled controls whether this OCSP server is consulted for revocation status, true or false, default false, so a new responder must be explicitly enabled. show ocsp-server-<name> returns url, enabled, priority and last-query, the timestamp of the last successful query. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application. Manage it with set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>] and show peer-certificate[-id] with attributes such as version, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, white-listed and revocation-mode. The white-listed flag, true or false with a default of false, means that if true the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain. status values are revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported, with in-use, unused and available deprecated in favour of valid plus the used-by tracking. revocation-mode is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto; alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default allowed.

SSH listens on port 8022 by default, and it is off by default: the enabled attribute, which enables direct access to shell via ssh, is true or false with a default of false. Configure with set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and read it back with show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. port is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell, a number in the range 1..65535, default 8022. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440, with no default. post-login-message is displayed after user login, also a string 0..1440, and defaults to a warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and that the service may be monitored. This object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key entry for that user; each entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], with set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>], show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label], and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>, which prompts for confirmation. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user, string 0..32; key-id is a unique identifier (name) for this entry, string 1..64. public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format as <key type><SPACE>base64 encoded OpenSSH public key<SPACE><comment>, a string of 0..2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is read-only and reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. label is a string 0..256.
